name: Zoe Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and everything you say is confidential. I'm interested in what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach Spanish and a bit of French at Riverside Community School, a mixed secondary of about a thousand kids. I'm in my second year. Most days it's four or five lessons, a lot of Year 7 and 8 learning to order food and describe their family, plus one GCSE Spanish group of only fourteen, because languages aren't popular. I use AI tools all day: I make listening exercises with AI voices, generate reading texts at the right level, and get quick feedback on kids' writing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment when a kid realises they can actually understand a Spanish song. What wears me out is the fight to keep the subject alive. Every year fewer kids choose languages at GCSE, partly because they say their phone can translate anything. My head of department, Mr Reyes, says we might go down from three language teachers to two next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, we all overreacted, and I'd post something funny about it, because I'm quite online. At work I'd tell the department we should use the time-saving bits and stop worrying. Publicly I'd sound relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even the boring version worries me, because translation apps already exist and they're already eating my subject. Kids don't need full AGI to decide Spanish is pointless. If the department goes from three teachers to two, I'm the newest, and that could happen whatever AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools to make lessons fun, because that's the best argument for keeping kids in languages. I'd start an after-school Spanish club with music and food to push GCSE numbers up. I'd also look at getting qualified to teach English as a second language, as a backup, maybe an online course for about £400.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not because of AI as such, because of my subject.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sound relaxed in public but you're worried. Why the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if the language teacher looks worried, the kids think the subject's dying, and then it does. Part of my job now is basically marketing Spanish to thirteen-year-olds. I can't do that with a long face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about money at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I live with my partner Freya, who's a software tester, and we split everything. We've got about four months saved together. If I lost my post, we'd be okay for a while, but Freya's job is the one I'd worry about in the other scenarios.

say: I'd post something funny saying **we all overreacted** about AI.
I'd tell the department to use the **time-saving bits** and stop worrying.
think: **Translation apps** are already eating my subject, AGI or not.
If the department **drops to two** teachers, I'm the newest.
do: Start an after-school **Spanish club** with music and food.
Take an online course in **teaching English** to second-language learners for about £400.
Keep using AI to make **lessons fun**.
feel: **Uneasy** about the future of her **subject**, not AI itself.
S0.quote: If the language teacher looks worried, the kids think the subject's dying, and then it does.
fieldNote: Her subject is **already shrinking** before AI changes anything.
She sees part of her job as **marketing Spanish** to pupils.
She'd hide worry in public to protect **pupil numbers**.

steps.text: Start an after-school Spanish club with music and food
Take an online course in teaching English as a second language
Use AI voices and texts to make Spanish lessons livelier

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say languages are about more than translation: culture, travel, meeting people. I'd post about it, and I'd tell parents at parents' evening. I'd be quite loud, because if I'm not, nobody else will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is the one where my post actually goes. If AI is translating and answering customers everywhere, the head and the parents will ask why kids need five years of Spanish. Language departments shrink, and I'm the junior one in a shrinking department. And Freya's job, testing software, is exactly the kind of checking work that goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the English as a second language course in the first six months and start teaching adults online in the evenings, a few hours a week. I'd talk to Mr Reyes now about what happens if they cut a post, so I'm not surprised. And Freya and I would stop saving for a holiday and put that into the emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Both our jobs feel shaky at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Freya say to each other that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit on the sofa and do a budget, because that's what we do when we're stressed. Freya would say she's fine and I'd know she's not. We'd probably agree that whichever of us lands something safe first, the other gets time to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools every day. Does that make it better or worse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better and worse. Better because I know what the tools can do, so I'm not scared of them. Worse, because I know exactly how good the AI tools are at the translation part of my job.

say: I'd say languages are about **culture and people**, not only translation.
I'd speak up at **parents' evening** and online.
think: My post could go as **language departments shrink**.
My partner's **software testing** job is exposed to the same checking tools too.
do: Finish the **English teaching course** within six months.
Teach adults **online in the evenings** a few hours a week.
Move holiday money into the **emergency fund**.
feel: **Anxious**, because **both jobs** in the household feel shaky.
S1.quote: I know exactly how good the AI tools are at the translation part of my job.
fieldNote: She's an **everyday AI user**, which makes her less scared but better informed.
The **household risk** doubles because her partner tests software.
She'd plan with her partner so **one retrains** while the other earns.

steps.text: Finish the English as a second language course in six months
Teach adults English online for a few evening hours a week
Move the holiday money into the emergency fund
Use AI to build adult English lesson materials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a huge deal and governments need to move faster than they ever have. I'd share serious stuff online for once, not memes. At school I'd try to stay steady for the kids, especially my GCSE group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm out of a teaching job by 2028 or soon after, at least as a Spanish teacher. If AI can do any thinking work, it can teach a language one-to-one better than me in a class of thirty. Freya's software testing job goes at the same time. Two years isn't enough for either of us to land on our feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast on anything with people at its heart. I'd look at becoming a form tutor and pastoral lead, or switching to primary, where it's more about looking after kids than content. I'd stop all spending that isn't rent or food and move our £5,000 savings into an easy-access account. And I'd talk to my parents about whether we could move back near them if we had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. My chest tightens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which is scarier, the 2028 date or the robots in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028, easily. Neither my partner nor I do hands-on work, so the robots don't really change our story. Freya says she might retrain as an electrician, which is mad, but in this world it would give her those extra three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your GCSE group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to finish the course, because learning Spanish changes how your brain works. I'd believe it, but I'd also know it might not get them a job. I'd want to be honest without frightening them.

say: I'd say governments must **move faster** than ever.
I'd stay steady for my **GCSE group** at school, even while scared.
think: I'm likely **out of work** as a Spanish teacher by 2028.
My partner's **testing job** goes at the same time.
do: Look at **switching to primary** or a pastoral lead role.
Cut all spending except **rent and food**.
Ask my parents about **moving back** near them.
S2.quote: Neither my partner nor I do hands-on work, so the robots don't really change our story.
fieldNote: Both earners in the household are in **thinking work**, so 2028 is the date.
Her partner jokes about becoming an **electrician** for the extra three years.
She'd consider **moving back** to her parents.

steps.text: Apply for primary teaching or pastoral lead posts
Cut spending to rent and food only
Move closer to her parents if both jobs go
Ask her parents for help with housing if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's still time to prepare if we start now, and I'd tell my department we need a plan, not just hope. I'd be a bit more measured online. I'd say languages should become about culture and confidence, not drills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still expect Spanish teaching to shrink, but five years lets me get across to something else before it does. By 2031 I'd want to be teaching in primary or in a pastoral role, where being a kind adult is the job. Freya would have time to retrain too, which takes a lot of pressure off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a primary teaching conversion course over the next two years, part-time. I'd keep using AI every day, so I can show any school that I'm the one who knows the tools. And we'd keep saving, maybe £200 a month, and hold off on buying a flat until 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. Five years feels like a plan instead of a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you give up Spanish entirely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it in my life, just not as my job. I'd teach it in a primary school as part of the timetable, maybe run a club. It's the kind of thing that would make me happy at thirty-five, so why not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from the school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly honesty. If the school is going to cut languages in 2029, tell me in 2027. A year's warning is everything.

I'd say languages should be about **culture and confidence**.
think: Five years lets me **move across** before Spanish teaching shrinks.
My partner could **retrain too**, which eases the pressure.
do: Do a part-time **primary conversion course** over two years.
Keep using **AI every day** to stand out.
Save **£200 a month** and delay buying a flat to 2030.
feel: Still **anxious**, but it feels like **a plan** rather than a fire.
S3.quote: If the school is going to cut languages in 2029, tell me in 2027.
fieldNote: She values **warning** more than anything else from her school.
Five years turns her plan into a **primary switch**.
She'd keep Spanish as a **hobby or club**, not her job.

steps.text: Take a part-time primary teaching conversion course
Keep using AI daily and show schools she knows the tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent warning, and that schools should plan a decade ahead for once. I'd write a long post about how language teaching could change. I'd sound hopeful, and mostly I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I can get properly good at teaching and build a second skill. I'd be thirty-seven by 2036, probably in primary or pastoral leadership. Spanish teaching still shrinks over the decade, but slowly enough for me to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching Spanish for a few more years, then switch to primary around 2030. I'd use AI tools to make my teaching better and to help the department. Freya and I would buy a flat around 2028, and maybe think about kids after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's a manageable kind of uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why still uneasy with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the end point's the same: my job as I know it still goes, just with more warning. I'd still have to change. And I worry about Freya, who's less keen on change than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help most in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Free retraining for teachers, and schools being honest about which subjects they plan to keep. If I knew in 2027 that languages would be cut by 2032, I'd plan around it.

say: I'd say **ten years** is decent warning for schools to plan.
I'd write about how **language teaching** could change.
think: Ten years lets me build a **second skill** by 2036.
Spanish teaching shrinks **slowly enough** for me to move.
do: Use **AI tools** to improve my teaching and help the department.
**Buy a flat** around 2028 and think about kids after.
S4.quote: The end point's the same: my job as I know it still goes, just with more warning.
fieldNote: She keeps the same **end point** in mind across all three AGI pictures.
Ten years lets her plan a **flat and family**.

steps.text: Move from Spanish to primary teaching around 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because both Freya and I do thinking work, so it hits our whole household at once. What would help is free retraining for teachers, and a guarantee that schools tell staff early which subjects they're keeping.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to languages as a skill. If AI translates everything, people stop learning other languages, and I think we'd lose something about understanding other countries. That's not just my job, that's bigger.

headlineQuote: If AI translates everything, people stop learning other languages, and I think we'd lose something about understanding other countries.
portrait: Zoe is a second-year **Spanish teacher** at a secondary where languages are already shrinking.
She uses **AI tools daily** and lives with her partner, a software tester, with about four months saved.
She sees **both household jobs** as thinking work, so the 2028 date hits hardest.
She plans a move into **primary teaching** and gets calmer as warning time grows.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it hits **both earners** in her household at once.
whatWouldHelp: Schools telling staff **early** which subjects they're keeping.
